front: Define skeletal (striated) muscle.
back: Tissue of bundles of contractile cells (myofibers) able to contract, produce body movement and maintain the position of body parts.

front: Name the four properties of muscle tissue.
back: Excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.

front: Give the levels of organization of skeletal muscle.
back: Muscle → fascicle → muscle fiber (cell) → myofibril → sarcomere → myofilaments (actin, myosin).

front: Connective tissue layers of muscle from outside in?
back: Epimysium (whole muscle) → perimysium (fascicle) → endomysium (each fiber) → sarcolemma (cell membrane).

front: Sarcolemma, sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum: what are they?
back: The muscle cell's plasma membrane, cytoplasm and smooth endoplasmic reticulum (stores Ca²⁺), respectively.

front: What is a T-tubule and what is a triad?
back: T-tubule: an inward folding of the sarcolemma that carries the action potential into the fiber. Triad: one T-tubule plus the two terminal cisternae beside it.

front: Define the sarcomere.
back: The smallest functional unit of striated muscle: the segment of a myofibril between two Z discs.

front: Which sarcomere bands shorten during contraction and which stays the same?
back: The I band and H zone shorten; the A band (length of the thick filament) stays the same.

front: Classify the sarcomere proteins by function.
back: Contractile: actin, myosin. Regulatory: troponin, tropomyosin. Structural: titin, nebulin, myomesin, dystrophin.

front: What are the three subunits of troponin?
back: TnC binds Ca²⁺; TnI inhibits actin–myosin binding; TnT binds the complex to tropomyosin.

front: What does titin do?
back: It runs from the Z disc to the M line, keeps the thick filament centered and acts as a spring that produces most of the passive tension when muscle is stretched.

front: Which muscle type lacks troponin and what replaces it?
back: Smooth muscle; Ca²⁺ binds calmodulin, which activates myosin light-chain kinase.

front: Compare initiation of contraction in skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle.
back: Skeletal: needs ACh from a somatic motor neuron. Smooth: stretch or chemical signals, can be autorhythmic. Cardiac: autorhythmic.

front: Which muscle type is fastest and which is slowest?
back: Skeletal is fastest, cardiac intermediate, smooth slowest.

front: List the five links from nerve to twitch.
back: Events at the neuromuscular junction → excitation–contraction coupling → Ca²⁺ signal → contraction–relaxation cycle → muscle twitch (sliding filament theory).

front: What happens at the neuromuscular junction?
back: The nerve AP opens Ca²⁺ channels → ACh release → ACh binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate → Na⁺ entry → end-plate potential → muscle action potential. Acetylcholinesterase breaks ACh down.

front: State the all-or-none principle for muscle.
back: A single fiber contracts fully once the stimulus reaches threshold and not at all below it.

front: How is the action potential coupled to Ca²⁺ release in skeletal muscle?
back: The AP travels down the T-tubule; the DHP receptor (voltage sensor) is mechanically linked to RyR1 on the SR, which opens and releases Ca²⁺.

front: How does Ca²⁺ switch on contraction?
back: Ca²⁺ binds troponin C → the troponin complex shifts tropomyosin off actin's myosin-binding sites → myosin heads bind and make a power stroke.

front: Describe the crossbridge cycle starting from rigor.
back: Rigor (head bound at 45°) → ATP binds, head detaches → ATP hydrolyzed, head cocks to 90° and binds weakly → Pi release triggers the power stroke → ADP released → rigor.

front: What are the three uses of ATP in contraction and relaxation?
back: Energy for the power stroke (hydrolysis cocks the head), detachment of myosin from actin, and pumping Ca²⁺ back into the SR (SERCA).

front: State the sliding filament theory.
back: Muscle shortens because thin filaments slide over thick filaments toward the M line; neither filament changes length.

front: How does skeletal muscle relax?
back: Nerve firing stops, ACh is destroyed, RyR closes, SERCA pumps Ca²⁺ back into the SR (bound by calsequestrin), Ca²⁺ leaves troponin and tropomyosin re-covers the binding sites.

front: Name the three pathways that regenerate ATP in muscle, with yield and duration.
back: Direct phosphorylation by creatine phosphate (1 ATP per CP, ~10–15 s); anaerobic glycolysis (2 ATP/glucose, lactic acid, ~30–40 s); aerobic respiration (~32 ATP/glucose, hours).

front: Give sport examples for each energy pathway.
back: Creatine phosphate: sprinting, weightlifting. Anaerobic glycolysis: tennis, football, 100 m swim. Aerobic: marathon, jogging.

front: Hypertrophy vs atrophy?
back: Hypertrophy: more actin and myosin (larger fibers), e.g. resistance training. Atrophy: loss of actin and myosin, from disuse, denervation or aging (sarcopenia).

front: Why does rigor mortis occur?
back: After death no ATP is made, so myosin heads cannot detach from actin: crossbridges lock in the rigor state. It is a physiological process.

front: What is a muscle cramp and how is it relieved?
back: A sudden, involuntary, painful sustained contraction from hyperexcitability of the somatic motor neuron; relieved by stretching. Triggers: electrolyte loss, heavy sweating.

front: Name the three factors that determine contraction strength.
back: Degree of stretch (length–tension), number of motor units recruited, and frequency of stimulation.

front: What is the optimal sarcomere length and why?
back: About 2.0–2.2 µm, where every myosin head can reach actin, giving maximal crossbridges and maximal active tension.

front: Active vs passive vs total tension?
back: Active: from crossbridges, maximal at optimal length. Passive: elastic recoil of stretched titin and connective tissue, rises with stretch. Total = active + passive.

front: Define a motor unit.
back: One motor neuron plus all the skeletal muscle fibers it innervates.

front: What is the size principle?
back: Motor units are recruited from smallest (fatigue-resistant) to largest (powerful, fast-fatiguing) as more force is needed (Henneman).

front: What is a twitch and what are its phases?
back: The response to a single stimulus: latent period (Ca²⁺ release), contraction phase (to peak tension), relaxation phase (Ca²⁺ pumped back).

front: What is treppe?
back: A stepwise increase in twitch strength with repeated stimuli of the same intensity, each given after complete relaxation (staircase effect of Bowditch), due to warm-up effects.

front: What is summation?
back: A new contraction beginning before the previous one has ended, so tension adds on top of the last; it increases with frequency.

front: Unfused vs fused tetanus?
back: Unfused (incomplete): partial relaxation between stimuli, wavy plateau with valleys. Fused (complete): no relaxation, smooth straight plateau at maximal tension.

front: What is fatigue and what are its two types?
back: A fall in force despite continued stimulation. Central (CNS, psychological/protective) and peripheral (NMJ, E–C coupling, Ca²⁺ signal, metabolite depletion and accumulation).

front: Isotonic vs isometric contraction?
back: Isotonic: muscle length changes (concentric shortening, eccentric lengthening) while tension is roughly constant. Isometric: tension develops without change in length.

front: How does load affect isotonic contraction?
back: Heavier loads lengthen the latent period and reduce shortening velocity and distance; when the load exceeds maximal force, the contraction becomes isometric.

front: Define a reflex.
back: A rapid, spontaneous, predictable motor reaction to a stimulus on a receptor, occurring without conscious control.

front: What makes a stimulus adequate for a reflex?
back: It suits the receptor, reaches threshold, is sudden and is not anticipated by the subject.

front: Name the five components of a reflex arc.
back: Sensory receptor → sensory (afferent) neuron → integration center → motor (efferent) neuron → effector.

front: Give four ways to classify reflexes.
back: By integration site (cranial vs spinal), efferent system (somatic vs autonomic), number of synapses (monosynaptic vs polysynaptic), development (innate vs learned).

front: Which reflexes are monosynaptic?
back: Only the stretch (tendon) reflexes, such as the knee jerk. Withdrawal and superficial reflexes are polysynaptic.

front: Describe the stretch reflex pathway.
back: Tap stretches the muscle spindle → Ia afferent → synapses directly on the alpha motor neuron of the same muscle → contraction; interneurons inhibit the antagonist (reciprocal inhibition).

front: Give the segments of the biceps, triceps, patellar and Achilles reflexes.
back: Biceps C5–C6, triceps C7, patellar L3–L4 (L2–L4), Achilles S1.

front: What is the normal response to the abdominal reflex?
back: Stroking each quadrant toward the midline makes the underlying muscles contract and the umbilicus move toward the stimulated side (T8–T12).

front: Direct vs consensual pupillary light reflex?
back: Light in one eye constricts that pupil (direct) and the other pupil equally (consensual), because the pretectal nuclei project to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei.

front: How are tendon reflexes graded?
back: 0 absent, 1+ diminished, 2+ normal, 3+ brisk, 4+ very brisk with clonus.

front: Hyperreflexia vs hyporeflexia?
back: Hyperreflexia (with clonus, Babinski) suggests an upper motor neuron lesion; hyporeflexia/areflexia suggests a lower motor neuron or reflex-arc lesion.

front: Why is a frog (Rana sp.) used in the wet lab?
back: It is poikilothermic (no temperature control needed), has a large gastrocnemius that is easy to prepare, and is easy to obtain.

front: Why is the frog pithed before the experiment?
back: To kill it humanely and destroy the brain and spinal cord so that CNS reflexes cannot interfere; limp hind legs confirm success.

front: What does a kymograph record?
back: Muscle shortening against time: a rotating drum turns time into horizontal distance, and a writing lever magnifies shortening into vertical deflection.

front: In PhysioEx, what happens as stimulus voltage increases?
back: No force below threshold (~0.8 V); force rises as more fibers are recruited, then plateaus at the maximal stimulus (~8.5 V).

front: In PhysioEx, why does 10 V give no more force than 8.5 V for a single twitch?
back: All fibers are already recruited at the maximal stimulus; further force needs higher stimulus frequency.

front: What is maximal tetanic tension?
back: The force reached when further increases in stimulus frequency no longer increase tension (≈140–150 stimuli/s in PhysioEx).
